## Knowledge and practical competence

Immediate knowledge scores can improve substantially without demonstrating durable competence. In [DiaPed](../../explorer.html#game-diaped), 40 children and adolescents improved from 29.8±6.02 to 68.6±1.58 out of 70. The uncontrolled design and near-maximum post-test score prevent attribution to the game alone and leave delayed transfer untested ([Atitallah et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1177/30502225251357044)).

The distinction also works in the other direction. In the six-month [Packy & Marlon trial](../../explorer.html#game-packy-and-marlon), 59 participants aged 8–16 showed improved reported self-care (*P*=.003) and parent communication (*P*=.025), but no between-group difference in knowledge or ==glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c)==. Self-efficacy (*P*=.07) and urgent-care use (*P*=.08) showed non-significant trends ([Brown et al., 1997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9183781/)). A knowledge test, family communication measure and clinical endpoint therefore answer different questions about the same game.

Population matters as much as the endpoint. The [Diabetic Mario](../../explorer.html#game-diabetic-mario) Android pilot enrolled 12 community children aged 9–13 without requiring diabetes. Its one-week questionnaire findings cannot establish efficacy in children with ==type 1 diabetes (T1D)== ([Baghaei et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1089/g4h.2015.0038)).

## Procedural distress and psychosocial learning

A focused intervention can support a more specific interpretation than a general claim of “better self-management”. In a randomised one-week study of 30 children, the [Koodak-e-Tavana injection game](../../explorer.html#game-koodak-e-tavana) reduced observed injection-related behavioural distress relative to control (*P*=.03). The endpoint was distress during a procedure, not independent injection competence or long-term coping ([Ebrahimpour et al., 2015](https://doi.org/10.5812/ijp.25(3)2015.427)).

[emoTICare](../../explorer.html#game-emoticare) instead addresses illness perception, emotional awareness and social skills. Its quasi-experimental study of 44 adolescents reported reduced perceived illness threat and preliminary socioemotional changes. The small non-randomised design does not establish a general treatment effect on diabetes distress ([Martín-Ávila et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2025.1668398)). These endpoints should remain distinct from empathy or recognition, the intended purposes of several unevaluated experiential games.

## Engagement: satisfaction and return use are different

In the two-arm [WeCan feasibility study](../../explorer.html#game-wecan), 20 of 31 intervention participants completed the programme, while 82% of responding participants reported satisfaction. Satisfaction among respondents is compatible with substantial non-completion; it is not a measure of retention for everyone recruited ([Wu et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pedhc.2024.05.009)).

The [Tangbao virtual-reality study](../../explorer.html#game-tangbao-superman) followed 54 children aged 4–9 for four weeks. It reported self-management-scale domain effects of 0.78–1.27 and a child usability score of 86/100. Its abstract's “95% session completion” differs from the body’s statement that 95% of children attended at least 10 of 12 sessions; the denominators cannot be treated as equivalent. With no comparator or biomedical endpoint, these results describe feasibility and measured change, not causal clinical benefit ([Gu et al., 2026; online 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-30114-1)).

## Glycaemic outcomes

Across mixed diabetes populations, seven studies with 607 participants produced a pooled HbA1c difference of −0.09 percentage points (95% confidence interval −0.29 to 0.10; *P*=.36). The same meta-analysis found a physical-activity standardised mean difference of 0.84 (95% confidence interval 0.30–1.38), but with high heterogeneity and interventions including active video games. That activity result cannot be transferred to sedentary glucose simulations ([Yao et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.2196/43574)).

The review included nine studies overall, with 913 participants, of whom 747 had type 2 diabetes. It required a glycaemic endpoint and searched through 1 April 2023. Its pooled estimate therefore answers a narrower question than whether games improve T1D learning or coping. The HbA1c confidence interval includes no difference and changes in either direction; it does not establish equivalence. Nor does a small favourable point estimate establish clinical benefit, despite more affirmative language in the review's discussion. The findings are best read as insufficient evidence of a pooled glycaemic advantage within the included interventions, rather than a verdict on every game mechanism ([Yao et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.2196/43574)).

The [eddii trial](../../explorer.html#game-eddii) provides a product-specific glycaemic signal. Of 92 randomised children with T1D aged 5–12, 70 entered the glycaemic analysis. The adjusted difference-in-differences in continuous-glucose-monitor time in range was +5.38 percentage points over six intervention weeks (*P*=.001). Non-random assignment of three replacement participants, post-randomisation exclusions, high baseline time in range and sponsor/author interests limit inference. The trial tested a particular data-linked interface, not educational transfer or every later eddii service ([Ahmadi and Lucero, 2025; online 2024](https://doi.org/10.1177/19322968231223759)).

A [Turkish trial](../../explorer.html#game-turkish-game-video-rct) with 55 children reported favourable quality-of-life and HbA1c differences after a **game-plus-animation** intervention. The available abstract does not provide effect magnitudes, and the game cannot be credited separately from the animation ([Tınmaz and Altundağ, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pedn.2025.01.023)).

## What the contrast between studies means

The intervention's route to an outcome matters. The eddii trial tested a gamified interface connected to actual glucose data; the injection study rehearsed a procedure; a glucose simulation instead asks learners to reason about represented physiology. A positive result for one route cannot validate the others. In particular, a behavioural effect produced while a tool remains in use is not necessarily knowledge retained after it is removed. These distinctions explain why the evidence should be synthesised by task and endpoint rather than reduced to a single “games work” conclusion.

Study exposure also changes the interpretation. A one-week reduction in procedural distress addresses an immediate clinical experience; a six-month behavioural trial addresses a longer period but may still have limited precision for infrequent outcomes. Conversely, an uncontrolled near-ceiling knowledge score can identify an educational signal while providing little information about which learner can apply the content independently. These are different evidentiary strengths, not a simple ordering by publication year or technical sophistication.

For designers, the clearest implication is to connect the repeated player action to the intended outcome. Rehearsing an injection sequence, explaining a delayed glucose response and practising disclosure to a peer should not share an undifferentiated success metric. The studies above support investigating these specific tasks; they do not establish that adding more mechanics, more realistic graphics or a more detailed physiological model improves learning. Such component-level claims require comparisons that actually manipulate those features.

## The unresolved question: transfer

The studies extracted here do not establish durable application to unfamiliar scenarios or everyday management. A later review of 23 paediatric T1D studies also found that sustained benefit remained inadequately established ([Guan et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-026-07142-5)). This is a limitation of the reviewed evidence, not proof that games cannot produce transfer.

For a causal-learning game, the useful next test is whether a learner can predict and explain an **unseen** scenario after a delay—not whether they can repeat a level they have practised. For a procedural or psychosocial game, assessments should match the intended skill or experience. The [evaluation chapter](../design/evaluation.qmd) sets out designs and instruments for these questions.

The [catalogue](../../explorer.html) contains the full product-linked sample, instrument, follow-up, result and appraisal records. [Methods and sources](../../methods.qmd) document the search limits and distinguish full-text from abstract-supported extraction.

## Abbreviation glossary

**HbA1c — Glycated haemoglobin:** a biomarker reflecting average glycaemia over approximately two to three months.

**T1D — Type 1 diabetes.**
